clinicalPearls: Develops after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease when loss of cortisol negative feedback allows the residual corticotroph adenoma to enlarge
The classic combination is progressive growth of an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour, very high plasma ACTH and skin hyperpigmentation
Hyperpigmentation results from markedly elevated ACTH and other pro-opiomelanocortin-derived peptides stimulating melanocytes
Mass effect may cause headache, visual field loss such as a bitemporal hemianopia, and hypopituitarism
Risk is higher in younger patients and in aggressive disease, and prophylactic pituitary irradiation at the time of adrenalectomy reduces the incidence
The condition is largely avoided by treating the pituitary source directly rather than relying on bilateral adrenalectomy alone
It is now less common as pituitary-directed therapy has become first-line for Cushing disease
Management combines transsphenoidal surgery and radiotherapy, and some tumours behave aggressively
reference.pathophysiology: Nelson syndrome arises when bilateral adrenalectomy, performed to control cortisol excess in Cushing disease, removes the cortisol that normally restrains the pituitary corticotroph adenoma. Freed from negative feedback, the corticotroph tumour grows and secretes large amounts of ACTH and other pro-opiomelanocortin derivatives. The excess ACTH and related melanocyte-stimulating peptides cause diffuse skin hyperpigmentation, while tumour enlargement produces local mass effects on the optic chiasm and the normal pituitary. Some corticotroph tumours in this setting are inherently aggressive, with rapid growth and, rarely, malignant transformation.
additionalDifferentials: Other sellar masses causing mass effect such as non-functioning adenoma, craniopharyngioma or meningioma
Primary adrenal insufficiency, which also causes hyperpigmentation and high ACTH
Persistent or recurrent Cushing disease before adrenalectomy
Other causes of hyperpigmentation such as haemochromatosis or drugs
additionalInvestigations: Serial plasma ACTH measurement, showing marked and progressive elevation
Serial pituitary MRI to document corticotroph tumour growth
Formal visual field assessment by perimetry for chiasmal compression
Assessment of remaining anterior pituitary function for hypopituitarism
Confirmation of adequate glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement after adrenalectomy
redFlags: Rapid tumour growth with visual field loss or cranial nerve involvement
Very high or steeply rising ACTH with deepening pigmentation
Features suggesting an aggressive or malignant corticotroph tumour
Adrenal crisis from inadequate replacement in an adrenalectomised patient
reference.prognosis: Variable: many corticotroph tumours are controlled with surgery and radiotherapy, but a subset behave aggressively with recurrence and rare metastasis; prophylactic radiotherapy and modern pituitary-directed treatment of Cushing disease have reduced the incidence and improved outcomes.
pitfalls: Relying on bilateral adrenalectomy without monitoring ACTH and pituitary imaging for tumour progression
Attributing new hyperpigmentation to under-replacement alone without imaging the pituitary
Missing visual field deterioration through infrequent monitoring
Overlooking the higher risk in children and young patients
references: Pituitary Society reviews on Nelson syndrome
